claims.text: Replacing high-energy laser melting with cold spray will reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Replacing high-energy laser melting with cold spray will improve the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Replacing high-energy laser melting with cold spray will reduce processing complexity.
The proposed cold-spray process uses a substrate temperature below 100°C.
AlCrFeNiSi particles can be accelerated to velocities sufficient for adhesion without melting.
Cold spray will retain the original AlCrFeNiSi powder microstructure.
Cold spray will minimize grain coarsening in deposited AlCrFeNiSi.
Cold spray will minimize phase transformations in deposited AlCrFeNiSi.
Retention of the powder microstructure will produce a low-stress microstructure with preserved alloy integrity.
Laser melting creates high thermal gradients.
Avoiding the thermal gradients of laser melting will retain fine microstructural features in AlCrFeNiSi.
Avoiding laser-melting thermal gradients will prevent thermal over-aging and coarsening.
Avoidance of high-temperature-induced flaws and phase transitions will lower residual stresses and improve mechanical properties.
Cold-sprayed components will have significantly lower residual thermal stresses than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Cold-sprayed components will have a finer and more stable microstructure than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Cold-sprayed components will have higher yield strength than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Cold-sprayed components will have higher hardness than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Laser powder bed fusion inherently imposes large thermal gradients and induces residual stresses.
Residual stresses generated by laser powder bed fusion often degrade mechanical properties.
The proposed processing window applies to millimeter-scale AlCrFeNiSi components deposited at near-ambient substrate temperatures.
